title: Salmon en Croute
subtitle: Salmon fillet with herbed cream cheese wrapped in puff pastry
excerpt: Salmon en croute is a salmon fillet spread with spinach and cream cheese, wrapped in puff pastry, and baked until golden. It is faster than a Wellington, works for a relaxed dinner as well as for entertaining, and the combination of cream cheese and spinach inside the pastry keeps the salmon from drying out.
sourceNotes: En croute (enclosed in pastry) is a French technique widely adopted in British cooking for salmon and other fish. The cream cheese and spinach filling is a modern British version, popular from the 1990s onward as a lower-effort alternative to a beef Wellington for entertaining.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble up to 8 hours ahead and refrigerate. Brush with egg wash just before baking. Do not freeze: the pastry becomes soggy as the salmon defrosts.

content.text: Salmon en croute is one of the more manageable pastry centrepieces: a salmon fillet, a layer of cream cheese and wilted spinach, all sealed inside puff pastry and baked for 25 to 30 minutes. It is less technically demanding than a Wellington because there is no pre-searing, no thermometer, and no layered wrapping stage. The salmon cooks gently inside the pastry in its own steam, which keeps it moist.

items.prepNote: one large piece, skin removed, pin-boned

content.text: Wilt the spinach in a dry pan over high heat, then squeeze out all the water firmly in a clean cloth. Chop finely. Mix with the cream cheese, lemon zest, and dill. Season generously.
Roll out the pastry into two rectangles slightly larger than the salmon fillet. Place one rectangle on a lined baking tray.
Spread half the cream cheese mixture down the centre of the base rectangle, in the footprint of the salmon. Place the salmon on top and spread the remaining cream cheese over the top and sides.

Brush the exposed pastry border with beaten egg. Drape the second pastry sheet over the top, pressing down the sides to seal. Trim to a neat rectangle with a 2 cm border. Crimp with a fork. Refrigerate for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 210°C fan. Score the pastry top lightly. Brush with beaten egg. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is golden and crisp. Rest for 5 minutes before slicing.

items.symptom: Pastry is soggy under the salmon
items.cause: Spinach was not squeezed dry enough before mixing into the cream cheese
items.fix: Wring the wilted spinach in a clean cloth very hard: it holds far more water than it looks. The filling should be thick, not wet, before assembly.

items.symptom: Salmon is overcooked and dry inside
items.cause: The oven temperature was too low and the cooking time too long
items.fix: 210°C fan for 25 minutes is usually sufficient for a 700 g piece. Check at 25 minutes by inserting a thin knife into the centre: it should feel warm but offer just a little resistance.

items.symptom: Pastry splits at the sides during baking
items.cause: The parcel was overfilled or the edges were not sealed firmly
items.fix: Use the fork or your fingers to press the edges firmly, then egg-wash to help the bond. Do not overfill: the filling expands slightly in the heat.

items.symptom: Filling leaks out of the ends
items.cause: Ends were not folded and sealed before baking
items.fix: Fold the pastry ends under the parcel and press flat before placing seam-side down on the tray. Egg wash the ends too.

content.text: Salmon en croute is a British dinner-party staple that has been in regular rotation since the 1980s. It is easier to pull off than a beef Wellington and more forgiving in timing: the salmon can rest in the pastry for a few minutes without the overcooking problem that beef presents. The cream cheese and spinach filling is a modern British invention; older French versions used a beurre blanc or plain herb butter. The herbed cream cheese version is the one most home cooks reach for today.
